Guided Inquiry

1 · Two motions in one quartic well

Let’s set the scene. A classical particle and a quantum wave packet are released together, at rest at x = +A, in the well V(x) = ½mω²x² + εx⁴. The pink dot is the Newtonian particle; the blue curve is |ψ(x,t)|², the probability of finding the quantum particle at x. The quartic strength ε sets how far the well departs from a pure parabola.

3 · Making every swing agree

Now let’s hunt for the culprit. Three quantities set this well: the mass m, the angular frequency ω and the quartic strength ε. Which change do you think makes the round-trip time the same at every amplitude?

The Physics

Anharmonic oscillator · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

A classical particle and a quantum wave packet are released together at the same point in the same well: a spring with a quartic stiffening term added. Following both shows how closely the quantum average tracks the classical motion, and how the quartic term changes that.

What you'll learn

  • How the round-trip time depends on the release amplitude A.
  • Which term in the well decides whether it does.
  • How the packet's width Δx behaves as the packet moves.
  • How the packet's mean position ⟨x⟩ compares with the classical position.
Where every run starts: the dot and the packet at x = +A. The dashed curve is the spring term by itself.

What's on screen

  • Potential V(x) (slate): the well, with its formula in the header.
  • Classical particle (pink dot): rides on the curve at its own x.
  • Quantum |ψ(x)|² (blue fill): the probability density, rescaled to fit the frame.
  • Ecl (gold dashed): the classical energy V(A), labelled with its value.
  • ⟨E⟩q (green dashed): the packet's mean energy, labelled with its value.
  • Statistics: classical x, ⟨x⟩ quantum, Δx (spread) and the clock. The Guided Inquiry reveals Δx and ⟨x⟩ step by step.
See itRelease both from rest at x = +A. Watch for: the pink dot running along the well and the blue density moving with it.

03

The well and the two travellers

The whole sim is one potential: a spring plus a quartic term. ε sets how much stiffer the well gets away from the centre.

The well V(x). At ε = 0 only the spring term is left.

Both travellers start at x = +A. The dot is at rest. The packet is a Gaussian centred on +A with zero mean momentum, with the width a pure parabola would keep unchanged:

The starting wave function. At the defaults Δx₀ = 0.62.

They do not start with the same energy. The dot has Ecl = V(A). The packet's mean energy ⟨E⟩q is higher, by ħω/2 (the zero-point energy) plus a share from the quartic term acting on the packet's width:

The gap between the green and gold lines at t = 0.

At the defaults ⟨E⟩q = 10.30 and Ecl = 9.23, a gap of 1.07, of which ħω/2 = 0.65. Both lines then stay put for the whole run.

See itRelease both and look at the two energy lines. Watch for: the green ⟨E⟩q label reading 10.3 and the gold Ecl label reading 9.2, with the green dashed line just above the gold one.
04

A wider swing takes less time

The classical force is the spring pull plus a cubic term:

The restoring force. The cubic term grows faster than the spring term.

At the turning point x = A the cubic term is 4εA²/(mω²) times the spring term: 0.43 at A = 3 and 1.70 at A = 6 (defaults). A larger swing is pulled harder than a spring would pull it, and that more than makes up for the longer path. A pure spring is different: its pull is proportional to the stretch, so any swing takes the same time.

Left: the force against the spring alone. Right: the round trip against A, at the defaults.

At the defaults one round trip takes 4.21 time units from A = 3 and 3.22 from A = 6. A spring alone would take 2π/ω = 4.83 at every amplitude.

See itTime one round trip from A = 3, then from A = 6, at the default m, ω and ε. Watch for: the second round trip finishing sooner, and the two times side by side in this card.
05

What sets the amplitude dependence

The round trip has an exact form. The substitution x = A sin θ removes the singularity at the turning point:

Exact for this well, not a small-ε expansion.

Dividing by ω shows that A enters only through λ = 2εA²/(mω²), which is half the force ratio of section 04. At ε = 0, λ = 0 and T = 2π/ω whatever the amplitude. For ε > 0, λ grows as A², so a wider swing is quicker. Changing m or ω does not remove this. It changes λ, and so how large the effect is. At ω = 4 (default m and ε), A = 3 and A = 6 take 1.55 and 1.48 against 2π/ω = 1.57.

m ω A ε

These sliders move the sim's own sliders, and each move restarts the run.

See itSet ε = 0 and time one round trip from A = 3, then from A = 6. Watch for: both round trips ending at the same time, 4.83.
06

The packet changes shape

The packet obeys the Schrödinger equation in the same well, with ħ = 1:

The packet's law of motion. The dot obeys Newton's law in the same V.

In a pure parabola the Gaussian start is a coherent state: a packet the parabola carries without distortion. It swings along the classical path with its width fixed, so Δx stays at 0.62 (defaults) for ever. With ε > 0 the energy levels are no longer evenly spaced, so the parts of the packet that sit in different levels drift out of step. The shape then changes: at the defaults Δx rises and falls over the first few round trips, and each peak is higher than the one before (about 1.0, 1.3, 1.5, 1.7).

See itFollow Δx for the first 5 time units at ε = 0, then at ε = 0.02. Watch for: Δx staying at 0.62 at ε = 0, and swinging between a low and a high value at ε = 0.02.
07

Why ⟨x⟩ stops following the dot

Ehrenfest's equations are exact for any packet:

d⟨x⟩/dt = ⟨p⟩/m     d⟨p⟩/dt = −mω²⟨x⟩ − 4ε⟨x³⟩

The dot obeys the same pair with ⟨x³⟩ replaced by ⟨x⟩³. They differ because ⟨x³⟩ = ⟨x⟩³ + 3⟨x⟩(Δx)² + ⟨(x−⟨x⟩)³⟩. For ε = 0 the ⟨x³⟩ term is absent and ⟨x⟩ follows the dot exactly. For ε > 0 the extra terms depend on the packet's width and skewness, so ⟨x⟩ drifts away from the dot.

At ε = 0.10, A = 3 and the default m and ω, Δx passes 2 by t ≈ 5. Then ⟨x⟩ shrinks towards 0 (it stays below 0.5 after t ≈ 7.5) while the dot still reaches ±3. ⟨x⟩ is an average over |ψ|². It is not the place where the packet is.

See itRun ε = 0.10 at speed 1 and compare the two position readouts. Watch for: within about 7 s, the ⟨x⟩ quantum readout shrinking towards 0 while Classical x still swings out to ±3.
08

Where it matters

  • Molecular vibration. A bond is a well that is nearly a parabola near its floor. The Morse form fitted to HCl puts its first two rungs 2885 and 2780 cm⁻¹ apart: the levels close up, which a pure parabola cannot do.
  • Superconducting qubits. A transmon is a slightly anharmonic oscillator. Its 1→2 transition sits a few hundred MHz below 0→1, so a microwave drive can address the lowest two levels alone.
  • Any real oscillator. Near the bottom every smooth well is a spring, and the corrections are what make real periods depend on amplitude.
Go deeper: a real bond
Computed from HCl's constants ωe = 2990.9 cm⁻¹ and ωexe = 52.8 cm⁻¹.
  • This sim's well is symmetric and stiffens, so its levels spread out. A bond softens at large stretch and its levels close up. The sign differs, the idea is the same.
  • A bond is also asymmetric: it resists compression more than stretching. That is what makes a solid expand on heating, and the sim's x⁴ well cannot show it.
09

Summary

In one line. A quartic term makes the round trip depend on amplitude and spreads the packet, so the packet's mean position stops matching the classical position.

Key points

  • V(x) = ½mω²x² + εx⁴. The packet's mean energy starts at Ecl + ħω/2 + 3εA²/(mω) + 3ε/(4m²ω²).
  • The round trip depends on A only through λ = 2εA²/(mω²). At ε = 0 it is 2π/ω.
  • At ε = 0, Δx is constant and ⟨x⟩ equals the classical x exactly.
  • At ε > 0, Δx changes, and ⟨x⟩ departs from the dot because ⟨x³⟩ ≠ ⟨x⟩³.

Common mix-ups

  • "Changing m or ω makes the period independent of amplitude." They rescale the time and change λ, but only ε = 0 removes the dependence.
  • "⟨x⟩ is where the particle is." It is an average over |ψ|², and it can sit where |ψ|² is small.
  • "The quantum packet should start at Ecl." It starts higher, by the zero-point energy and the quartic share.

Things to try on your own

  • At the defaults, find the amplitude, in steps of 0.5, whose round trip is closest to 4.0 time units.
  • Set ε = 0.10 and A = 3. Read the time after which |⟨x⟩| stays below 0.5.
  • Set ω = 4 and compare the round trips at A = 3 and A = 6 with those at the defaults.
